content: Cyclohexane is a cycloalkane with the molecular formula C6H12. It is widely used in the chemical industry as a nonpolar solvent and as a precursor in the production of adipic acid and caprolactam, which are intermediates in the synthesis of nylon. Industrially, cyclohexane is synthesized by the catalytic hydrogenation of benzene. Its unique chemical and conformational properties make it valuable in laboratory settings for analytical purposes and as a standard reference compound. The molecular structure of cyclohexane does not conform to a flat, planar hexagon. A planar hexagonal structure would result in significant angle strain because the bond angles would deviate from the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5°, and torsional strain would arise from eclipsed bonds. To minimize these strains, cyclohexane adopts a three-dimensional chair conformation, which is its most stable form. In this conformation, the carbon atoms are arranged such that the bond angles are approximately 109.5°, and the hydrogens are positioned either in the plane of the ring (equatorial) or perpendicular to it (axial). This arrangement minimizes both angle and torsional strain, making cyclohexane the most stable cycloalkane with essentially zero ring strain. Another conformation, known as the boat conformation, also exists but is less stable and readily interconverts to the chair form. When cyclohexane is substituted with a bulky group, the substituent preferentially occupies an equatorial position to further reduce steric hindrance. Cyclohexane is chemically inert under standard conditions due to its nonpolar and hydrophobic nature. However, it can undergo reactions with extremely strong acids, such as the superacid system HF + SbF5, which can induce protonation and hydrocarbon cracking. Substituted cyclohexanes, on the other hand, exhibit reactivity under various conditions, which is of significant importance in organic chemistry. The spatial arrangement of substituents on cyclohexane derivatives plays a critical role in their chemical reactivity, particularly in reactions involving nucleophiles. For example, in the elimination reaction (E2) of bromocyclohexane with a hydroxide ion (OH−), the bromine substituent must be in the axial position, opposite an axial hydrogen atom, to facilitate the reaction. During the reaction, the bond between the carbon and bromine breaks, releasing Br−, while the hydroxide ion abstracts the adjacent axial hydrogen, forming water (H2O). Simultaneously, the electrons from the C-H bond form a double bond between the two carbon atoms, resulting in the formation of cyclohexene. This reaction predominantly proceeds via the E2 mechanism, yielding cyclohexene as the major product (~70%), although competing substitution (Sn2) reactions can also occur under certain conditions. In the Sn2 pathway, the bromine is replaced by a hydroxyl group, which quickly reverts to the more stable equatorial position. Commercially, most cyclohexane is oxidized catalytically to produce a mixture of cyclohexanone and cyclohexanol, commonly referred to as KA oil. This mixture serves as a precursor for the production of adipic acid and caprolactam. The relative proportions of cyclohexanone and cyclohexanol in KA oil can be adjusted by selecting appropriate oxidation catalysts, which in turn determines whether the mixture is more suitable for adipic acid or caprolactam synthesis. Additionally, cyclohexane is used as an organic solvent in various applications. In research, cyclohexane continues to be a subject of interest. Studies on cyclohexane-benzene mixtures and solid-phase cyclohexane aim to explore their hydrogen yields under irradiation at extremely low temperatures (−195 °C), contributing to advancements in chemical and material sciences. Historically, cyclohexane was not readily available from natural sources like coal, unlike benzene. Early chemists relied on organic synthesis to obtain it. In 1867, Marcellin Berthelot reduced benzene with hydroiodic acid at high temperatures, mistakenly identifying the product as n-hexane due to its boiling point and his incorrect assumption that benzene was not a cyclic molecule. In 1870, Adolf von Baeyer repeated the experiment and identified the product as hexahydrobenzene. Later, in 1890, Vladimir Markovnikov claimed to have distilled the same compound from petroleum, naming it hexanaphtene. However, in 1894, Baeyer successfully synthesized cyclohexane through a Dieckmann condensation of pimelic acid followed by multiple reduction steps. That same year, E. Haworth and W.H. Perkin Jr. synthesized cyclohexane via a Wurtz reaction of 1,6-dibromohexane. Interestingly, their cyclohexane had a higher boiling point than the previously identified compounds. In 1895, Markovnikov, N.M. Kishner, and Nikolay Zelinsky resolved this discrepancy by determining that the earlier compounds were actually methylcyclopentane, formed through an unexpected rearrangement reaction.
